title: The Budapest Gambit
description: A fun counterpunch against the Queen's Gambit by White, and a bit more solid than the Albin. Also features a trap which can win you the game in less than 10 moves!

r1b1kb1r/pp1ppppp/4nn2/q7/1PQ2B2/2N5/P1P.text:
White sidesteps.

We'll just retreat the queen, leaving the f4-bishop under attack.

r1b1kb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/q1n5/1P1Q1B2/2N5/P.text:
This move is a fork, but we can deliver a fork of our own.

The crafty Ne6 fits the bill.

r1b1kb1r/pp1ppppp/n4n2/q1P5/3Q1B2/2N5/PP.text:
Play can continue with developing a piece and blocking the check.

We'll regain the pawn.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2p1p/3b1np1/5p2/3P4/1BN1PN2/.text:
And we castle. It seems our knight will have a good home on e4 after it gains the support of the rook.

It might be useful to push ...c6 and prevent White from accessing the d5-square.

r1bqk2r/pppn1p1p/3b1pp1/8/3P4/1BN1P3/PP3.text:
The bishop retreats.

We'll continue our plan to exert control over e4.

r1bqk2r/pppn1p1p/3b2p1/5p2/3P4/1BN1PN2/P.text:
White develops.

And we'll complete the knight maneuver.

r1bqkb1r/1p2pppp/p2p1n2/2n5/4PB2/2N2P2/P.text:
The queen develops and prepares castling queenside.

b5 is very natural.

r1bqkb1r/4pppp/p2p1n2/1pn5/4PB2/2N2P2/PP.text:
White castles.

We'll fianchetto the bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2n5/4PB2/5P2/PPP3P.text:
e4 comes.

We'll stake a claim to the center by playing d6.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/n4n2/2P5/3Q1B2/8/PPP1P.text:
Trying to defend doesn't work.

We have a check on a5.

r1bqkb1r/pp1ppppp/n4n2/2P5/5B2/5P2/PPP1P.text:
White wants a big center.

We'll take on c5.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/3p1n2/2n5/4PB2/2N2P2/PP.text:
White develops the knight.

Now a6 is a good multi-purpose move, preventing any white minor piece from accessing b5, and preparing for queenside expansion and fianchettoing the c8-bishop.

r1bqkb1r/pp2pppp/3pnn2/4B3/1PQ5/2N5/P1P1.text: But we can still bully it. Our pieces are quite well placed. Our bishop is coming to d7 and if white takes on f6, we'll recapture with our g-pawn, opening the file for our rook.

r2q1rk1/p1n1ppbp/1p3np1/2ppN1B1/P2P4/2P1.text:
a4 covers the b5 square.

We'll attack the bishop.

r2q1rk1/p3ppbp/np3np1/2ppN1B1/3P4/2P1P3/.text:
The knight arrives to a good square: e5.

Our knight is slightly offside, so we'll bring it back towards the center.

r2q1rk1/pb1n1pbp/1p1p1np1/4P3/P4B2/2PB1N.text:
White can't win a pawn because of the undefended d3-bishop.

We recapture, opening the d-file.

r2q1rk1/pb1n1pbp/1p3np1/4B3/P7/2PB1N1P/1.text:
This is just an example.

We'll exchange on e5.

r2q1rk1/pb1nppbp/1p1p1np1/2p5/3P1B2/2PBP.text:
The rook enters the e-file, perhaps in preparation for pushing the e-pawn. 

We can opt for a similar plan.

r2q1rk1/pb1nppbp/1p1p1np1/2p5/P2P1B2/2PB.text:
White expands on the queenside. The pawn does well to control b5.

We'll take on d4.

r2q1rk1/pb1nppbp/1p1p1np1/8/P2P1B2/2PB1N.text: White opens up the e-file a bit more for the rook. But here, keep an eye out: sometimes e5 is tactically warranted!

r2q1rk1/pb3p1p/1p4p1/4N3/P4n2/2PB3P/1P3P.text: And we can jump to f4, attacking the bishop and the pawn on g2. We also have dangerous ideas of Qg5.

r2q1rk1/pb3pbp/1p3np1/4N3/P7/2PB3P/1P1N1.text:
White recaptures, defending the bishop. 

Now we can play ...Nh5, when the white minor pieces are suddenly rather loose.

r2q1rk1/pb3pbp/1p4p1/4N2n/P7/2PB1N1P/1P3.text:
A second knight joins the defensive chain.

Our g7-bishop is good here, but we'll take on e5 for a very specific tactical reason.

r2qk2r/pp1n1p2/2pbbpp1/3p3p/3P3P/4P1P1/P.text:
It seems White really wants c4.

We'll inhibit it with Nb6.

r2qk2r/pp3p2/1npbbpp1/3p3p/3P3P/1P2P1P1/.text:
White wants to go c4. But in preparing it with b3, we now have induced weakened dark squares that we'll be able to infiltrate with our bishop!

First, let's get our queen out.

r2qkb1r/1b2pp1p/p2p1np1/1pn5/4PB2/2N2P2/.text:
And now we prepare the double fianchetto. 

All in all, it seems our pieces will have pretty good squares, and White will be taken out of their London System comfort zone, since they won't face a traditional queen's pawn opening setup.

We can castle short and get control of the c-file.

r2qr1k1/1b3pbp/pp3np1/2p1p3/4P3/2PB1N1P/.text: The middle game will largely consist of queenside play, now that the center is practically closed with two e-pawns facing each other.

r2qr1k1/pb1n1pbp/1p1p1np1/2p1P3/4PB2/2PB.text:
White takes.

We can recapture and stay active.

r2qr1k1/pb1nppbp/1p1p1np1/2p5/3PPB2/2PB1.text:
White pushes in the center as planned.

And we'll strike back at the white center with ...e5.

r2qr1k1/pb3pbp/1p1p1np1/2p1B3/4P3/2PB1N1.text:
White trades off the strong knight.

We'll take back, and the d3-bishop is momentarily under attack from our queen.

r3k2r/pp2qp2/1np2pp1/3p1b1p/3P3P/bP2P1P1.text: And finally this move completely prevents the plan of c4, which White had been preparing. We'll be castling queenside next and going g5, with the added benefit of having neutralized White's counterplay! The rook on b1 looks misplaced.

r3k2r/pp2qp2/1npbbpp1/3p3p/3P3P/1P2P1P1/.text:
White castles, in preparation for the forthcoming middle-game battle.

We'll disrupt any intended c4 advance by kicking the c1-rook.

r4rk1/p1q1ppbp/1p2nnp1/2ppN3/P2P3B/2P1P3.text: And finally we connect rooks. Our play could continue with opening the c-file, or perhaps offering a trade of knights on e4, depending on how White wants to continue!

r4rk1/pbqn1pbp/1p1p1np1/4p1B1/P2P4/2PB1N.text: But we step out of the way and our queen is developed, our rooks are connected, and e5 is on the board!

rn1q1rk1/pb1pppbp/1p3np1/2p5/3P1B2/2PBPN.text:
White castles.

White usually wants to invade the e5-square so it is a good idea to  defend it now.

rn1q1rk1/pb2ppbp/1p1p1np1/2p5/3P1B2/2PBP.text:
White gives the bishop a retreat square.

We'll bring our knight out and support a potential pawn break with ...e5.

rn1qk2r/pb1pppbp/1p3np1/2p5/3P1B2/2PBPN2.text:
The bishop comes out to d3.

And we'll get castled.

rn1qk2r/pp3p1p/2pbbpp1/3p4/3P4/4P1P1/PPP.text:
White develops the other knight.

Let's gain some space and expand on the kingside.

rn1qk2r/pp3p2/2pbbpp1/3p3p/3P3P/4P1P1/PP.text:
White prevents us from pushing forward.

We'll develop our last minor piece.

rnb1kb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/q1P5/5B2/4P3/PPP2.text: We'll regain the pawn with a check, though.

rnbq1rk1/p3ppbp/1p3np1/2pp2B1/3P4/2PBPN2.text:
White castles.

Now we can continue with our plan. The d3-bishop is pinned against the rook.

rnbq1rk1/pp2ppbp/5np1/2pp2B1/3P4/2PBPN2/.text:
Defending.

We'll get ready to bring out our queen's bishop. The idea is to exchange off the good bishop on d3.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p2B1/3P4/3BPN2/P.text:
Developing the bishop.

We'll strike at the white center.

rnbqk2r/p2pppbp/1p3np1/2p5/3P1B2/2P1PN2/.text:
White develops the knight.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/pp1pppbp/5np1/2p5/3P1B2/2P1PN2/P.text:
White continues with their London pawn structure.

We'll prepare a second fianchetto.

rnbqk2r/pp3p1p/2pb1pp1/3p4/3P4/4P1P1/PPP.text:
White develops the b1-knight.

We'll bring out our queen's bishop, in preparation for completing our queenside development.

rnbqk2r/ppp1ppbp/5np1/3p2B1/3P4/4PN2/PPP.text:
White settles for e3.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/ppp2p1p/3b1pp1/3p4/3P4/4P1P1/PPP.text: White develops and attacks the d-pawn, which we'll support with c6.

rnbqk2r/ppp2p1p/3b1pp1/8/2BP4/2N1P3/PP3P.text:
Developing the knight.

We'll get our knight out as well. We have a plan of Nd7, f5, Nf6, bringing it to a location where it will have a strong influence upon the center.

rnbqk2r/ppppppbp/5np1/6B1/3P4/5N2/PPPNPP.text:
White develops another knight.

We'll play d5 and prevent White from playing e4.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2P5/5B2/4P3/PPP2P.text:
This option is always present for White. The f1-bishop already covers the a6 square, so the knight can't come out to a6 in this variation. 

In this position, White takes only 3% of the time.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppp1p/5np1/2p5/3P1B2/4PN2/PP.text:
White continues developing the pieces normally.

We'll complete the fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2P5/5B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
Taking is also very logical. 

It's played 8% of the time.

But we're regaining the pawn with Na6.

rnbqkb1r/pp1ppppp/5n2/2p5/3P1B2/4P3/PPP2.text:
White defends the pawn and plays e3 now that the bishop is out of the pawn chain. 

This is the most popular move, played 54% of the time.

We'll prepare to fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/3p4/2PP4/4P3/PP3PP.text: White undermines our center, but trading is our plan.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/3p4/3P4/4P1P1/PPP2.text:
White prepares to fianchetto 13% of the time here.

Because of the strong central white pawn chain, we are now going to reposition our bishop on d6, encouraged by the idea of a future h4 targeting the white kingside.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2p1p/5pp1/8/2BP4/4P3/PP3PPP/.text:
White recaptures.

d6 is a good, active location for our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/5pp1/8/3P4/4P3/PPP2PPP.text:
White places pawns on dark squares and supports d4.

We'll place our d-pawn in the center.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5Bp1/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/.text:
The bishop trades itself off, damaging our structure slightly.

Our f-pawns are doubled.

rnbqkb1r/pppppp1p/5np1/6B1/3P4/5N2/PPP1P.text:
White continues with normal development 8% of the time.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/6B1/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
The Trompowsky is also another possible early deviation. 

It's only played 4% of the time, since there are so many second moves possible.

That's still almost 8.5 million games!

We'll prepare our kingside fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/3P1B2/8/PPP1PPPP.text:
Black now has to face The London. 

You'll face it 15% of the time (it's played in almost 33.5 million games).

There are many ways of playing against the London, but for the purposes of this course we are going to challenge the central white pawn with 2...c5.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
The Budapest Gambit is a great choice if you want to surprise your opponent very early in the game and get a fighting position. 

Firstly, let's take a look at what happens if White goes for the Trompowsky or the London, as this poses a change for our setup.

2kr1b1r/pp1n1ppp/2p2q2/4nb2/2P2N2/2N1P3/.text:
White castles.

They needed to get their king into safety but now we'll attack the queen.

2kr1b1r/pp3pp1/2p2q2/2n1nb1p/2P2N2/2N1P3.text: And we attack on the kingside! White is in a precarious position!

4rrk1/pppnq1pp/3b4/3P1p2/5P1n/2N1P2P/PP1.text:
And we bring another rook to the center.

White's pawn on e3 is definitely a target, and we have great control over the e4-square, providing us with some central space.

r1b1k2r/ppp2pp1/2np1q1p/8/2P5/2P1P3/P1Q2.text:
White opens up their bishop.

We'll attack the white queen.

r1b1k2r/pppp1pp1/2n2q1p/8/2P5/2P5/P1Q1PP.text:
The queen defends.

Next, we'll make room to get our bishop out.

r1bq1rk1/1pp2ppp/3p1n2/p1nPp3/2P1P3/P7/1.text: And we can get castled. We have two really well placed knights in the resulting position, and we can even dream about jumping to h5 into f4 at some point, or even pushing f5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2n2n2/8/1bBP4/2N2N2/PP3.text:
White castles.

Let's put pressure on d4.

r1bqk2r/1pp2pbp/2np2p1/p1n5/2P1PP2/2N2N2.text: The bishop is fianchettoed. We'll castle, develop the bishop, and our pieces have active squares.

r1bqk2r/1ppp1ppp/5n2/p1nPp3/2P1P3/P7/1PQ.text:
White defends the e4-pawn.

We'll prepare to get the bishop out.

r1bqk2r/1ppp1ppp/n4n2/p2Pp3/2P1P3/P7/1P1.text:
White releases their bishop.

And our knight comes to c5, attacking the e-pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1pp1/2n2B1p/8/2P5/2P5/P3PPPP.text:
The bishop takes our knight.

We'll get our queen out, hitting c3.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/6B1/1bP5/2N5/PP2P.text:
White elects to pin us, too.

We'll take on c3 and damage their pawn structure.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/6B1/2P5/2P5/P3PPP.text:
Recapturing.

We'll take steps to break the pin on our knight.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2p1p/2np2p1/p1n5/2P1PP2/2N2N.text: Pushing the pawns and expanding in the center.

r1bqkb1r/1pp2ppp/2np4/p1n5/2P2P2/2N1PN2/.text:
The knight is developed.

We'll fianchetto.

r1bqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np4/2n5/2P2P2/4PN2/PPB.text:
White wants to keep their bishop.

Let's restrict the white queenside.

r1bqkb1r/pppn1ppp/2np4/8/2P2P2/3BPN2/PP4.text:
White castles.

We'll push the bishop back.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n2n2/8/2P5/2N5/PP2PPP.text:
The queen retreats.

We'll bring our bishop out and pin the knight.

r2q1rk1/pppn1ppp/3b2n1/3P4/5P2/2N1P2P/PP.text:
Play can continue with f4.

We'll play f5, preventing White from expanding in the center with e4, and fixing the backward e-pawn.

r2q1rk1/pppn1ppp/3b4/3Pn3/8/2N1P2P/PP3PB.text:
White castles.

Now that White has committed the king, we should take measures to occupy vulnerable squares in front of the castled position.

r2q1rk1/pppn2pp/3b2n1/3P1p2/5P2/2N1P2P/P.text:
The king clears a square for the rook.

Let's bring our knight to a dangerous outpost.

r2q1rk1/pppn2pp/3b4/3P1p2/5P1n/2N1P2P/PP.text:
The rook is placed opposite our king.

We connect our rooks.

r3k2r/ppp2pp1/2np1q1p/5b2/2P5/2PBP3/P1Q2.text: If the bishop blocks, trading is the right idea here.

r3k2r/ppp2pp1/3p1q1p/4n3/2P5/2PQP3/P4PPP.text: And we bring our knight to the center, with a better position and the superior pawn structure.

r3kb1r/pp1n1ppp/2p2q2/4nb2/2P2N2/2N1P3/P.text:
Developing the knight.

We'll castle queenside, setting up potential discoveries on the d-file against the queen.

r4rk1/ppp2ppp/2nq1n2/8/1bBP2b1/2N1BN2/PP.text: And we connect rooks, getting ready to bring them to the center and keep adding pressure to the d4-pawn.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/2np4/p1b5/2P1PPb1/P1NBB.text:
Proposing a trade.

Let's make it harder for White to trade off our strong bishop and centralize our knight.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/3p4/p1b5/2P1PP2/PnNBBP2.text:
But more importantly, we'll likely have a dark-squared bishop trade and we'll control the c5-square to put a knight there.

We have a dynamic position.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/3p4/p1b5/2PnPP2/P1NBBP2.text: After the capture on f3, White's structure is compromised.

rn1q1rk1/1pp2ppp/3p4/p1b5/2PnPPb1/P1NBBN.text:
The only move for White is now Qf2 to save the queen and keep the minor pieces defended.

We'll take on f3 with the bishop.

rn1q1rk1/ppp2ppp/3b4/3Pn3/8/2N1P2P/PP3PB.text:
The bishop is placed on the diagonal supporting d5.

We continue to play actively.

rn1qk2r/ppp2ppp/3b4/3Pn3/8/2N1P2P/PP3P1P.text:
White supports their center.

We'll castle.

rn2kb1r/pp3ppp/2p2q2/4nb2/2P2N2/4P3/PP2B.text:
White prepares castling.

We continue to develop our minor pieces.

rnb1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/8/2P1PP2/2P1B1P1/P6.text: We retreat and attack e4. Our knight will develop to a6 soon.

rnb1kb1r/pp3ppp/2p2q2/4n3/2P2N2/4P3/PP3P.text:
White retreats to d1.

While playing a gambit, developing is key.

rnb1kb1r/ppp2ppp/5q2/3Qn3/2P2N2/4P3/PP3P.text:
The knight is transferred to f4.

We'll attack the queen and force it away from the center.

rnbq1rk1/1pp2ppp/2np4/p1b5/2P1PP2/P1NB1N.text:
The queen is developed, perhaps supporting a Be3 move to trade our strong bishop.

We'll bring our bishop out, pinning the knight and threatening the disruptive Nd4.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2pbp/3p2p1/4n3/2P2N2/2N1P3/P.text: And we support our knight on e5. Also, our other knight is coming to c5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/2b5/2P1PP2/P1NB1N2.text:
White prepares b4.

So we clamp down on this idea by playing a5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/1bP1PP2/4BN2/PP1.text:
Now we get castled. 

Our pieces won't have any problems getting developed and our king got castled faster than White's.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/1bPP4/2NB1N2/PP.text:
White develops the light-squared bishop.

Now we can take on c4, and the bishop has to lose a tempo.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/2PP4/2N5/PP1Q1P.text: We just castle, with a slightly more comfortable position.

rnbq1rk1/ppp2ppp/5n2/8/1bBP4/2N2N2/PP3PP.text:
The bishop recaptures.

We'll continue our development.

rnbqk2r/1ppp1ppp/5n2/p2Pp3/2P5/P7/1P1NPP.text:
The knight recaptures.

We'll bring our b8-knight out, eyeing the useful square c5.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/3p1n2/3Pp3/2P5/2P5/P3PPP.text: And we're left with a better structure.

rnbqk2r/ppp2ppp/5n2/3p4/1bPP4/2N2N2/PP3P.text:
Play can continue with Nf3.

We'll castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp1pbp/6p1/4n3/2P2N2/2N1P3/PP3.text:
On f4 the knight has a good home.

Let's castle.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b5/2P1PP2/3B1N2/PP.text:
The bishop is developed to d3.

We'll play d6, preparing to get the other bishop out.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bP1PP2/2N1B3/PP4.text:
White blocks with the knight.

We'll capture, doubling White's pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/1bP1PP2/4B3/PP1N2.text:
The knight blocks on d2.

We'll prepare to activate our queenside.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2P1PP2/2P1B3/P5PP.text:
White recaptures.

Let's check the white king.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/3Pp3/1bP5/2N5/PP2PP.text:
Blocking with the knight isn't so good.

Let's exchange and double the white pawns.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/3Pp3/1bP5/8/PP1BPPP.text:
White can block and propose a trade.

We can support our bishop here favorably. If White takes, our rook will be unleashed on the a-file.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/1bPP4/2N5/PP3PPP/.text:
White usually blocks with the knight here.

Let's continue actively in the center.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/1bPP4/8/PP1B1PPP/.text:
The bishop blocks and proposes a trade.

At this point, players choose this move 47% of the time.

We'll exchange.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP1Q1PPP/R.text:
The queen recaptures.

We'll push in the center.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/2np4/8/2P2P2/3BPN2/PP4P.text:
White develops their bishop, facing our kingside.

We'll bring out our b8-knight. It can come to c5 and pester the white bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3Pn3/8/4P2N/PP3PPP/RN.text:
The pawn captures.

This is actually the most common move, played 37% of the time.

We can now split the White pawn structure on the kingside. While this involves giving up the bishop pair, it means that when White castles kingside, the king will be more exposed than normal.

rnbqkb1r/ppp2ppp/8/3Qn3/2P5/4P2N/PP3PPP/.text:
White grabs the pawn with the queen.

Naturally, we don't exchange queens.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1p1p/6p1/4n3/2P5/2N1P2N/PP3.text:
The knight is developed to h3.

Our bishop comes out.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2P1PP2/4B3/PP4PP.text:
White develops the bishop. 

We will develop as well, to the usual square.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2P1PP2/5N2/PP4PP.text:
The knight is developed to f3.

The difference is that our bishop will occupy the c5-square as opposed to the b4-square.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/8/2P2P2/4PN2/PP4PP.text:
White continues with development.

We'll prepare a pathway to get our queenside pieces out.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/3Pp3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP.text:
White simply advances the pawn 18% of the time.

Developing is the answer.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
White plays the conventional capture. 

It's by far the most common move.

You'll see it 52% of the time, which is more than 4.5 million games!

We'll bring our knight to g4, where it attacks the e5-pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
Nc3 does nothing about the tension between the pawns, but develops a knight.

It's chosen 17% of the time.

We'll capture on d4.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4p3/2PP4/4P3/PP3PP.text:
e3 supports d4.

Expect to see this move 7% of the time.

We should trade and develop with a tempo yet again.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP3PPP/RN.text:
White recaptures.

We'll check the white king.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/8/2PQ4/2N5/PP2PPPP.text:
White recaptures.

We can develop and attack the white queen.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/2P1P1n1/8/PP3PPP.text:
White opens up an attack on our knight and places another pawn in the center.

4.e4 is only played 6% of the time, but has some merit to it.

We'll take on e5.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/2P3n1/4P3/PP3PPP.text:
White opens up an attack on our knight only 4% of the time, but it makes sense as a move.

We take on e5.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/2P1PP2/8/PP4PP/R.text: Expanding and chasing our knight away.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/2P2P2/4P3/PP4PP/.text:
Attacking our knight in the middle.

This move is actually played 20% of the time.

People just love attacking knights in the center with pawns.

Let's retreat, but still allow for the g6 and fianchetto plan.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/2P5/2N1P3/PP3PPP.text:
White can also develop to c3.

We'll fianchetto.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4n3/2P5/4P2N/PP3PPP/.text:
The knight is headed to f4. 

We should insist on our gambit play here, with d5!

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White adds another pawn to the center.

We offer our gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
You've reached the third study of the Budapest Gambit. 

In this study, White will actually allow us to enter the first moves of the gambit! 

However, they'll start deviating on move 3. We'll explore a conventional-looking 3. dxe5, but without the logical continuations of Nf3 and Bf4.

1bbqr1k1/1p3p1p/2p2p1r/p2p1Q2/2P5/1P2P1N.text: And we've got d5, opening an attack on the queen and freeing up our position.

2b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/3p2nr/p1b5/2P2N1q/1P2P2P.text: This simple retreating move encourages an exchange, but if White takes it they'll be lost! Rxg6 will be too much pressure. White needs to tread carefully.

2b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/3p3r/p1b1n3/2P2N1q/1P2P2.text: And we play d6, consolidating our pieces.
Simple moves don't work for White.

2b1r1k1/1ppp1ppp/7r/p1b1n3/2P2N1q/1P2P2P.text:
White defends.

And we play d6, consolidating our pieces. It also means we have a bishop sacrifice on h3 if the knight leaves f4!

2bqr1k1/1pp2ppp/3P4/p7/2P5/1P2b3/PB2B1PP.text: And we capture a pawn in the center. Our bishop is a monster around the king!

2bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/7r/p1b1n3/2P2N2/1P2P3/P.text:
The knight goes back to defend.

Our queen comes in, threatening immediate mate!

2bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/r7/p1b1n3/2P1N3/1P2P3/P.text:
Attacking our bishop with the knight.

Our bishop retreats to safety.

2bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/r7/p1bNn3/2P5/1P2P3/PB2.text:
The knight moves up to d5.

But this allows us immediate kingside pressure.

2bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/r7/p1bQn3/2P5/1PN1P3/PB.text:
Attacking our bishop.

Our bishop can slide back to a7.

2bqr1k1/bp1p1p1p/2p2p1r/p4Q2/2P1N3/1P2P3.text:
The queen stays on the kingside, applying pressure.

We'll attack h2.

2bqr1k1/bp1p1p1p/2p2p1r/p7/2P1N3/1P1QP3/.text:
The queen retreats.

Moves like d5 are possible. White cannot take.

2bqr1k1/bp1p1ppp/2p2B1r/p2Q4/2P1N3/1P2P3.text:
This is a crazy response, but quite possible.

Now our pawns are damaged.

2bqr1k1/bp3p1p/2p2p1r/p2P4/4N3/1P1QP3/P3.text: This reply doesn't spot our threat. In this middle game, we have some tricks!

2bqr1k1/bpp2ppp/3P4/p4r2/2P5/1P2P3/PB2B1.text:
White takes.

We capture the rook.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/5r2/p3nN2/2P2P2/1P2P3/P.text:
A move like f4 opens up White too much on the kingside.

We take the knight.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/7r/Q3n3/2P1N3/1P2P3/PB2.text:
Let's see what happens if White grabs the a5-pawn.

Our bishop is attacked, so we'll move it to b6 and counterattack the white queen.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/7r/p2QB3/2P1N3/1P2P3/P3.text:
Was the knight free?

We can displace the queen from the defense of the bishop.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/7r/p3nN2/2P5/1P2P3/PB2B.text:
The knight can gain a tempo on our rook.

But we can gain the tempo back on the knight.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/8/p3Pr2/2P5/1P2P3/PB2B1.text:
White recaptures ours. They're left with isolated doubled e-pawns, and e3 is already loose.

Now d6 begins to undermine the pawns. We also defend our f5-rook.

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/r7/p2Qn3/2P1N3/1P2P3/PB.text:
The knight moves up, adding another attacker on our e5 knight.

We don't have to defend it!

2bqr1k1/bppp1ppp/r7/p3n3/2P5/1P2P1N1/PB2.text:
The knight is transferred to the kingside.

We bring our attacker across.

3qr1k1/bp3p1p/2p2p1r/p2P1b2/4N3/1P1QP3/P.text: As we're winning a piece if this happens.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/1b1p3r/2P1B3/4N2q/1P2P3.text:
The bishop takes, temporarily defending h2.

After recapturing, our threats will remain.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/1b5r/2P1p3/4N2q/1P2PP2/.text:
f3 defends the knight.

We'll take on h2.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/1b5r/2P1p3/4N2q/1P2PPP1.text:
White blocks.

But now we return to h2.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/1b5r/2P1p3/4N3/1P2PP2/P.text:
White is totally lost.

We give another check, further exposing the opponent's king.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp2ppp/1b5r/2P1p3/4N3/1P2PPP1/.text: The king is back to the square he began the game on.

Q1b1r1k1/1pp3pp/1b5r/2P1pp2/4N3/1P2PPP1/.text: And we attack the piece that defends g3. This is an example of an attack you could get even deep in a main line of the Budapest Gambit, despite your opponent knowing the best ten moves.

Q1bqr1k1/1pp2ppp/1b1p3r/2P1n3/4N3/1P2P3/.text:
c5 seems clever, trying to wreck our structure.

Should we ignore it?

Let's threaten mate on h2 and, at the same time, the knight on e4!

Q1bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/1b5r/4n3/2P1N3/1P2P3/P.text:
The queen moves down to a8, trying to do some damage.

We'll prepare to get our queen's bishop out. We are not afraid of the white queen.

r1b1k2r/1p2qppp/p1pp4/2b1n3/2P1Q3/2N1P3/.text:
And we're playing ...a6 before ...f5. We want to have a safe square for our dark-squared bishop. 

We'll play ...f5 and ...0-0 in the next few moves. White won't have any advantage at all. In fact, they'll have a problem piece: the dark-squared bishop.

r1b1k2r/pp1pqppp/2p5/2b1n3/2P1Q3/2N1P3/P.text:
Qd1 was also popular, but it really poses no problems. 

Against Qd1, we can go for normal development.

But against Qe4, there's a nice idea I want you to remember: ...d6 to play ...f5.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/2bQP3/2P3n1/2N1PN2/.text:
Nc3 is now the most popular move, with the simple idea of development.

But now we can take the e5-pawn and have ideas of ...c6 to kick the queen out.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/2bQN3/2P3n1/2N1P3/PP3.text:
You'll most likely see a trade here.

But we just bring our other knight back into the center.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/2bQn3/2P5/2N1P3/PP2BP.text:
White may prepare castling.

But now we can make use of the ...c6 move which also controls the d5- and b5-squares. 

The c3-knight now doesn't have access to these squares.

r1bq1rk1/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2P3n1/4PN2/P.text:
White castles, too.

We'll bring our rook to the half-open e-file.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2P3n1/4PN2/PP.text:
White just develops the bishop 23% of the time. There is no way to defend the e-pawn.

We can simply castle, as we don't need to rush to regain the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/2bQP3/2P3n1/4PN2/PP.text:
White could try this move, attacking the bishop on c5 and defending e5 for one more turn. 

They will try it 15% of the time.

However, after Qe7 we deal with both ideas. We're going to be taking on e5 soon.

r1bqr1k1/1ppp1ppp/8/p1b1n3/2P5/1PN1P3/PB.text:
White fianchettoes.

An added benefit of ...a5 before any other pawn pushes is that we can reroute our rook to the kingside!

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1N3/2P5/2N1P3/PP.text:
This is an option White may have.

We recapture.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1P3/2P3n1/2N1PN2.text: The white knight is developed, but we have enough pieces attacking the e5-pawn and will just capture it.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/2n5/2b1n3/2P5/1PN1PN2/.text:
b3, supporting c4 and giving the c1-bishop a square to fianchetto is a good move.

We trade a pair of knights.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/8/2b1n3/2P5/1PN1P3/P3B.text:
The dark-squared bishop needs a place to go.

It is always a good idea to grab some space on the queenside in this line of the Budapest.

r1bqr1k1/pppp1ppp/8/2b1n3/2P5/1PN1PB2/P4.text:
We attack the bishop. 

This will force the bishop back. 

The position seems to have transposed back into the main line.

rnbqk2r/pppp1ppp/8/2b1P3/2P3n1/4PN2/PP3P.text:
White blocks the attack. At the same time, it's good we provoked this move because the dark-squared bishop is trapped behind the pawns.

We'll continue to go for rapid development, attacking the e5-pawn once more.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
And so they take it!

We'll play our knight to g4, attacking the e-pawn as before.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/2P3n1/5N2/PP2PPP.text:
The knight defends the recent pawn acquisition. 

You'll come across 4.Nf3 by far the most often, with 54%.

It's played in more than 2.1 million games.

Let's develop and attack f2.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White adds a second pawn to the central battle.

We'll offer our gambit.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
This is a study on one of the main lines of the Budapest Gambit: 4. Nf3.

As you can see by the title of this move, White brings their knight out early. 

The purpose of this is to defend the pawn they have recently acquired by accepting our gambit. 

The games can continue with fairly equal evaluations, but Black always has very aggressive ideas that can result in powerful attacks!

1R6/p1p2kpp/3p4/3n4/2bP1B2/6P1/r4P1P/4R1.text: We've already taken a few pawns for it, and our light-squared bishop will be very strong and unopposed.

1r4k1/p1p3pp/3p1n2/3B4/2bP1B2/6P1/r4P1P/.text:
While this check wins an exchange for White, we will have enough compensation for it in the form of pawns and piece activity.

We take the bishop.

1r4k1/p1p3pp/3pbn2/8/2PP1B2/5BP1/P1r2P1P.text: But we can afford to leave our rook on an active square, attacking the queenside pawns.

1r4k1/pBp3pp/3pbn2/8/2PP1B2/6P1/P3rP1P/1.text:
White's rook defends.

We'll take on a2.

1r4k1/pBp3pp/3pbn2/8/2PP1B2/6P1/r4P1P/1R.text:
White attacks our bishop.

We'll take on c4. White had set up a nasty trap. The natural reply Kf7 would have lost to 20.Rxe6 Kxe6 21.Bd5+.

1rb1k2r/p1p2ppp/1p1p4/4Q3/2P5/P3P3/1P3PP.text:
White is in a simplifying mood!

We recapture.

1rb1k2r/p1p2ppp/1p6/4p3/2P5/P3P3/1P2BPPP.text:
White develops. Now there'll be no need to castle as we are close to the endgame.

Black has more freedom to bring out the king.

3r1rk1/p1p1qppp/1pb5/n3p3/2P5/2P1PN2/P1Q.text: We place our bishop actively. The c-pawns are a permanent liability.

3r1rk1/p1pbqppp/1p6/n3p3/2P5/2P1PN2/P1Q1.text: White places their rook on the file, too.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/3p4/2P1n3/5B2/Pp2P3/1Q2.text: c5 to undermine our defense of e5.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/3p4/4n3/p1P2B2/PNb1P3/1.text: The queen prefers to capture, keeping the structure sound.

r1b1k2r/1pp1qppp/3p4/p3n3/1bP2B2/1N2P3/P.text: The idea is to control squares around the bishop.

r1b1k2r/1ppnqppp/3p4/8/2P2B2/PQP1P3/4BPP.text: But we reroute our knight, where it'll dominate the destroyed queenside pawns!

r1b1k2r/2ppq1pp/1p3p2/4n3/P2Q1B2/2P1P3/5.text:
White expands on the queenside.

We fianchetto.

r1b1k2r/p1p2ppp/1p1p4/3Qq3/2P5/P3P3/1P3P.text:
Proposing a trade.

We'll move our rook and leave the onus on White to exchange queens.

r1b1k2r/p1pp1ppp/1p6/4q3/2P5/P3P3/1P1Q1P.text:
Putting pressure on d7.

With that in mind, we push the d-pawn to d6 where it is supported by the c-pawn.

r1b1k2r/p1ppq1pp/1P3p2/4n3/3Q1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
White captures, taking the opportunity to rid themselves of one of their weak c-pawns.

We recapture, opening the a-file for our rook.

r1b1k2r/ppp1q1pp/2np1n2/8/2P2B2/2PQ1NP1/.text:
White can continue with a fianchetto.

Now castling is sensible.

r1b1k2r/ppp1qppp/2np4/4n3/2PN1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
Nd4 hopes for an exchange, but we won't do it.

We'll just castle.

r1b1k2r/pppp1ppp/8/4q3/2P5/P3P3/1P1Q1PPP.text:
White is ready to develop their 
bishop.

We'll prepare to fianchetto.

r1b1k2r/ppppq1pp/2n2P2/3Q4/2P2Bn1/2P2N2/.text:
White captures.

Our knight returns to f6, attacking the white queen.

r1b1k2r/ppppq1pp/2n2n2/8/2P2B2/2PQ1N2/P3.text:
The queen retreats, defending the two weak c-pawns.

We'll prepare to get our bishop out.

r1b1k2r/ppppq1pp/5p2/2P1n3/3Q1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
White makes use of the pawns, trying to restrict our options for pawn play on the queenside.

We'll develop our bishop on b6.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/3QP3/2P2Bn1/2P2N2/P.text:
White defends the attacked e5-pawn.

It is impossible to add an attacker to it without giving up another pawn. This is completely fine, as getting active pieces is more important.

We play in gambit style and push f6!

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4N3/2P2B2/2P1P3/P4P.text:
White chooses to exchange knights.

We recapture.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/1bP2Bn1/4PN2/PP.text: White prepares to develop the light-squared bishop and castle.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/1bP2Bn1/P4N2/1P.text:
White puts pressure on our bishop 43% of the time.

Definitely a logical move.

This allows us to set up a trap, however.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4P3/2P2Bn1/2P1PN2/P.text:
e3 seems less challenging.

We simply regain the pawn.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4n3/1PP2B2/5N2/1P1N.text: Grabbing on b4 is a huge blunder.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/2n5/4n3/2P2B2/2P1PN2/P3.text:
White defends the knight and develops the bishop.

We support our knight as well.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/4B3/1bP5/P7/1P1NPPPP/.text:
Another trade?

We need to save our bishop before recapturing.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/4B3/2P5/P7/1P1QPPPP/R.text:
The queen recaptures.

And our queen does likewise.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/4n3/1bP2B2/P3P3/1P1N1.text:
White defends against the checkmate threat.

Our bishop was under attack. We trade.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/4n3/2P2B2/P3P3/1P1Q1P.text:
The queen recaptures.

d6 is a standard move in these positions.

r1b1k2r/ppppqppp/8/4n3/2PQ1B2/2P1P3/P4PP.text:
Adding another attacker.

We defend with the f-pawn.

r1b1r1k1/ppp1q1pp/2np1n2/8/2P2B2/2PQ1NP1.text:
White allows us to regain the pawn by capturing on e2.

The queens are going to be exchanged. Let's see how this works out.

r1b1r1k1/ppp1q1pp/2np1n2/8/2P5/2PQBNP1/P.text:
The bishop blocks our attack on the e2-pawn.

But we can target the bishop with our knight!

r1b1r1k1/ppp1q1pp/2np4/6B1/2P3n1/2PQ1NP1.text:
Attacking our queen.

We'll move the queen to an active location on f7, where it takes aim at both f2 and c4.

r1b1r1k1/ppp2qpp/2np4/2P3B1/6n1/2PQ1NP1/.text:
White tries to undermine our structure, but our pieces get active in the meantime!

Let's hop into the center with the c6-knight!

r1b1r1k1/ppp2qpp/3p4/2P1N1B1/6n1/2PQ2P1/.text: White exchanges a pair of knights, but leaves f2 to be taken.

r1b1r1k1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/8/2P2B2/2P2NP1/P3.text:
White recaptures.

Our rook arrives on the seventh.

r1b1r1k1/ppp3pp/3p4/2P1n1B1/8/2PQ2P1/P2K.text: We recapture. White's position has fallen apart. You should take care of business after this.

r1b2rk1/1pp1qppp/3p4/1Nb1n3/2P2B2/P3P3/P.text: We just retreat. c6 is coming.

r1b2rk1/2p1qppp/1p1p4/p3n3/2P2B2/PP2PP2/.text:
White defends.

We'll bring the bishop out.

r1b2rk1/p1p1qppp/1p1p4/4n3/2P2B2/P3PP2/1.text:
Perhaps an effort to make Bb7 less effective.

We'll take steps to restrain the queenside expansion idea of b4, and prepare to attack the c4-pawn with Ba6.

r1b2rk1/p1p1qppp/1p1p4/n3B3/Q1PN4/2P1P3/.text:
Attempting to diminish the pressure.

But when we take back with the pawn, White still has problems.

r1b2rk1/p1p1qppp/1p6/n3p3/Q1P5/2P1PN2/P3.text:
The knight goes back.

We attack the queen.

r1b2rk1/ppp1q1pp/2np1n2/8/2P2B2/2PQ1NP1/.text:
The bishop goes to g2.

We'll double on the half-open e-file.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qppp/2np4/4n3/2PN1B2/2P1P3/P.text:
White castles, too.

The c-pawns are bad. We'll start to target them.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qppp/3p4/4n3/2P2B2/P3P3/1P1Q.text:
And so does White.

Our bishop is coming to b7.

r1b2rk1/ppp1qppp/3p4/n3n3/Q1PN1B2/2P1P3/.text:
White defends and attacks us.

We'll simply support the knight with the b-pawn.

r1b3k1/ppp3pp/2np1n2/8/2PN1B2/2P3P1/P3rP.text:
And now White forces us to fix their structure.

We have little choice but to take on d4.

r1b3k1/ppp3pp/3p1n2/8/2PP1B2/6P1/P3rPBP/.text:
The pawn structure has been repaired, and White's pressure on the queenside is immense.

Rather than defend passively, we offer our b7-pawn in order to get our remaining pieces out.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP2Bn1/2N2N2/P.text:
Blocking with the knight on c3 is also possible.

And it's played half the time.

We'll take on c3 and double the white pawns.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/1bP2Bn1/5N2/PP1.text:
White blocks with a knight 49% of the time.

We bring the queen out and attack the pawn once more.

r1bqk2r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/2P2Bn1/2P2N2/P3.text:
They recapture.

Our queen comes to e7 to put pressure on the weak e5-pawn.

r1bqkb1r/pppp1ppp/2n5/4P3/2P2Bn1/5N2/PP2.text:
White brings another defender.

And we check. The idea is to develop our bishop before playing Qe7.

r3k2r/1bppq1pp/1p3p2/4n3/P2Q1B2/2P1P3/5K.text: We just retreat, up a pawn with a better position.

r3k2r/1bppq1pp/1p3p2/4n3/P2Q1B2/2P1PP2/6.text:
A natural move like f3, controlling the center, fails...

White can't recapture as the knight would give a fork when capturing f3.

r3k2r/1p2qppp/4b3/4p3/8/Pp2P3/1Q3PPP/R2B.text: White really wants to take the pawn back.

r3r1k1/1bp1q1pp/1p1p1p2/p1n5/2P1P3/PPQ2P.text: And we create a pawn wall of dark-squared pawns. We don't have a dark-squared bishop, so this is a sound strategy!

r3r1k1/1bp1qppp/1p1p4/p3n3/2P5/PP2PPB1/3.text:
The white rook steps to the e-file, too.

We'll maneuver our knight to c5, in the process uncovering an attack on e3.

r3r1k1/1bpnqppp/1p1p4/p7/2P1P3/PP3PB1/3Q.text:
White pushes the weak pawn forward.

Now we bring our knight to c5, attacking b3.

r3r1k1/2p1qppp/bp1p4/p3n3/2P5/PP2PPB1/3Q.text:
That's why the bishop must move.

The c4-pawn is now secure, so we'll bring our bishop to the long diagonal.

r4rk1/2p1qppp/bp1p4/p3n3/2P2B2/PP2PP2/3Q.text:
White places themselves in a defensive position, keeping everything secured.

We'll start to activate our rooks, placing the f8-rook on the half-open e-file and planning Ng6.

r4rk1/p1pbqppp/1p6/n3p3/2P5/2P1PN2/P1Q1B.text:
The queen retreats to c2.

Our rook enters the open file.

r4rk1/pbp1qppp/1p1p4/4n3/1PP2B2/P3P3/3QB.text: We fianchetto. So from here on you should analyze this position and the plans you could organize. Keep in mind you can go Nd7/a7-a5/Ra7/Rfa8, or if you're brave, you can play f5 and g5 and attack on the kingside!

r5k1/pBp3pp/3pbn2/8/2PP1B2/6P1/P3rP1P/R4.text:
White grabs the pawn.

We'll attack the bishop. The c4-pawn is also under fire.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/5n2/4P3/2P5/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
White accepts it.

We jump forward and attack the pawn.

rnbqkb1r/pppp1ppp/8/4P3/2P2Bn1/8/PP2PPPP.text:
Now White defends it with the bishop.

4.Bf4 is opted for 20% of the time, equating to almost 780000 games!

We add another attacker.

rnbqkb1r/pppppppp/5n2/8/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Placing a second pawn in the center.

We play the Budapest Gambit!

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Let's look at important lines with 4.Bf4. What if White chooses to take their bishop out and defend the pawn?

Well, it's another option. Hanging onto the pawn will only be possible for a couple of moves, since we'll play the moves we have prepared. 

As you'll see from the continuations, too, there are chances for us to develop an attack, even in the middle game.
